Since the launch of the PlayStation 5 in late 2020, hundreds of games have been released on the console. Some titles are PS5 exclusives , so the only place to play them is on PlayStation itself and, in some cases, on PC. Others are cross-platform with ports for the Switch 2 , Xbox Series X |S, and more.

Still, the best PS5 games to play are those that highlight the capabilities of the PlayStation 5 and its newer models, the PlayStation 5 Slim and PlayStation 5 Pro . All these consoles can hit up to 120Hz in 4K, depending on the title, and include the DualSense , a top PS5 controller that features haptic feedback, adaptive triggers, and more. Plus, a PlayStation Portal , PlayStation VR2 , and other PS5 accessories can make PS5 games even more immersive and enjoyable to play.

Below are all the current PS5 games. Everything from AAA titles and remasters of classics to upcoming PS5 exclusives and exciting multi-platform releases, such as Until Dawn 2 and Grand Theft Auto VI , is included.

articles.title: Party Plots Walkthrough - Hello Kitty Island Adventure Guide - IGN
articles.summary: After completing the Quest Dream Homes Part 2 and successfully building Island Homes for Chococat, Cinnamoroll, Pochacco, and Tuxedosam, it's time to
articles.body:
After completing the Quest Dream Homes Part 2 and successfully building Island Homes for Chococat, Cinnamoroll, Pochacco, and Tuxedosam, it's time to celebrate your accomplishments! In Party Plots, the next Quest in Hello Kitty Island Adventure's Welcome Home update , you will help My Melody throw a party and decide which characters will be getting Island Homes next!

Before you can begin the Quest Party Plots, you must complete the following requirements:

Raise your Player Home to at least Level 3, which will occur when you have built 7 Character Homes.

Complete the Quest Comic Relief , which unlocks Hangyodon and the Comedy Club.

Reach the following Friendship Levels by giving characters daily Gifts: Friendship Level 6 with Hangyodon Friendship Level 7 with Pompompurin Friendship Level 8 with Pekkle

Once you have completed all of the above steps, you can begin Party Plots by talking to My Melody. She can typically be found in her shop, Small Gift, Big Smile.

When you talk to My Melody, she says that she wants to throw a party to celebrate Marroncream and help everyone get to know her better. However, she's taken on too many tasks as usual and needs your help!

Head to the Comedy Club in Rainbow Reef and talk to Hangyodon. You will find him discussing Island Homes with Pekkle and Pompompurin. You agree to help the three of them out, and receive Construction Plans for their Island Homes. Hangyodon also happily agrees to host the party at the Comedy Club.

Find My Melody next to the Nature Preserve Fast Travel Mailbox in Spooky Swamp and talk to her there. She tells you that everything is ready to go for the party, as Cinnamoroll will find Marroncream and give her an invitation.

When My Melodyleaves, Kuromi and Badtz-Maru show up and tell you they want to investigate Marroncream to learn more about her. You aren't sure about helping them, but they insist. Gather the following materials:

Box Clamx 10 - found in Rainbow Reef, possible Fwishing Well reward, reward for playing the Seapony Racing mini-game

Coral Spores x 5 - obtained when recycling Trash at the Recycling Plant in Rainbow Reef

After gathering the necessary items, gift them to Badtz-Maru. Badtz-Maru and Kuromi tell you that they will construct a hiding place and use it to sneakily spy on Marroncream.

The Quest concludes here - My Melody's party for Marroncream does not actually happen yet. Instead, it's time to put those Construction Plans to use and build some more Island Homes for your friends!

articles.title: Game show do Enem: Estudantes testam conhecimentos no sábado (31) | G1
articles.standfirst: Estudantes de quatro escolas estaduais de tempo integral participam de desafios que ajudam na preparação para o exame.
articles.summary: Estudantes de quatro escolas estaduais de tempo integral participam de desafios que ajudam na preparação para o exame.
articles.body:
Game show do Enem: estudantes testam conhecimentos em programa que estreia neste sábado (31) — Foto: TV Clube

O game show Ingresso Universitário estreia neste sábado (31), na Rede Clube, logo após o programa Piauí de Riquezas. Apresentado pela jornalista Stephanie Pacheco, a atração reúne estudantes de escolas públicas estaduais do Piauí em uma competição de conhecimentos gerais com foco na preparação para o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem).

A nova temporada reúne alunos de quatro Centros Estaduais de Tempo Integral (Cetis), divididos entre os grupos Azul e Amarelo . A proposta é ajudar os estudantes a revisar conteúdos cobrados no Enem de forma leve e descontraída.

O time Amarelo é formado por estudantes do Ceti Raldir Cavalcante Bastos e do Ceti Governador Dirceu Mendes Arcoverde. Já o time Azul reúne alunos do Ceti João Henrique de Almeida Sousa e do Ceti Liceu Piauiense.

Nesta edição, o programa terá novas dinâmicas, mais perguntas e comentários de professores parceiros. Eles vão explicar as respostas e ajudar o público a compreender os conteúdos apresentados.

Segundo Ludson Andrade, gerente de marketing da Rede Clube, a proposta é unir entretenimento e aprendizado. Com isso, os telespectadores também poderão revisar conteúdos importantes para o Enem.

"Nossa intenção é que o público consiga absorver conhecimento de forma divertida, no conforto de casa. Este ano, a competição vem com mais perguntas e comentários de professores parceiros, que vão explicar as respostas de forma didática", destacou Ludson.

*Yngridy Vieira, estagiária sob supervisão de Ilanna Serena.

Throughout Phantom Blade 0, you'll collect a massive list of weapons from defeating bosses and completing side quests. Each weapon has its unique skills and combos to learn. Clicking on any of the weapon links in the table below will take you to a new page that provides more details on each specific weapon.

You'll need to level up each weapon individually by collecting upgrade materials found around each zone of Phantom Blade 0. You can reset a weapon's level to refund all of your materials, which makes it easier to experiment with different options.

You'll find a large chunk of these weapons on the main story route, but just enough of them are off the beaten path, so be sure to keep a close eye on this list as you continue through Phantom Blade 0.

Weapons can also be upgraded to increase their stats and even unlock unique abilities and new playstyles. You can refund all of your Remnant Dust and upgrade materials for free up to level 10; after level 10, you'll need a Weapon Reforge Talisman.

articles.title: The Fanatic's Broken Blade - Phantom Blade Zero Guide - IGN
articles.summary: The Fanatic's Broken Blade is a much more complicated weapon in Phantom Blade 0 than any other weapon you've encountered thus far. The blade has a
articles.body:
The Fanatic's Broken Blade is a much more complicated weapon in Phantom Blade 0 than any other weapon you've encountered thus far. The blade has a standard five-hit combo and a three-hit Sha-Chi combo.

The Fanatic's Broken Blade's ability changes the entire property of the weapon.

While Sober, Press L2 to consume 1 Sha-Chi essence, unleash [Flying Sword Flurry], and enter the Tipsy stat. This attack is unblockable.

While Tipsy, press L2 to consume 1 Sha-Chi Essence and enter the Drunk state for 20 seconds. While drunk, mobility is greatly restricted and L1 cannot be used to block. However, Soul automatically dodges incoming attacks, and [Flying Sword] damage is greatly increased.

While Drunk, press L2 again to unleash [Empowered Flying Sword Flurry] without consuming Sha-Chi Essence and return to the Sober state. This attack is unblockable.

How to get The Fanatic's Broken Blade in Phantom Blade 0

You'll obtain the Fanatic's Broken Blade after defeating Hua Qianxiao in the Crimson Forest.

As you level up The Fanatic's Broken Blade, you'll gain access to new abilities. Below, you'll find all the additional powers the one-handed sword will gain.

articles.title: Hua, Deadly Betrothed - Phantom Blade Zero Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Hua, Deadly Betrothed is an optional boss in the Weeping Creek Valley in Phantom Blade Zero. She is found as a part of the Flesh Lily side quest.
articles.body:
Hua, Deadly Betrothed is an optional boss in the Weeping Creek Valley in Phantom Blade Zero . She is found as a part of the Flesh Lily side quest.

Hua has several deadly mechanics in her moveset that can be hard to manage at first. But learning how she fights, behaves, and how her poisonous flowers work will make the fight easier to tackle.

Beyond the three main mechanics of the fight, Hua is largely an endurance fight, asking you to parry sword attacks, and continuously maintain your parry timing to wear down her Sha-Chi meter . She will also constantly teleport around the arena after combos, in-between combos, and before starting her attacks towards you, requiring you to be constantly on the ball.

These are the key moves and mechanics you need to learn and watch out for:

You can slink in-between them as they spin, but be warned if you hit one, you will get stunned and fall to one knee, opening you up for a grab attack.

Parry these just as she swings her sword down to deal a lot of Sha-Chi damage and open Hua up for a combo.

She can also perform this attack on its own. It will deal remove about 60% of your health if you get caught by this attack.

With this fight, you want to learn the parry timings over dodging, unless dealing with the various flowers she spawns and landing one or two hits in-between combos and at the end of attack chains. We suggest using the Sanguine Reach weapon, due to its range and impressive combos as you won't always be right next to Hua due to the amount of moving around she does.

When her Sha-Chi meter has been depleted, this gives you a key opportunity to land a heavy attack combo. When her Sha-Chi meter is around half full, you can also use a fully charged Dread Axe Phantom Edge attack to deal a massive chunk of health damage.

Simply repeat this over and over by continuously stunning Hua until you outlive the amount of poisonous flower attacks she spawns and deplete her health. Chances are you will make it through this fight by the skin of your teeth.

Upon defeating her, you will get the Scarlet Wraithblade weapon, which allows you to spawn those same deadly flowers from your own attacks.

You can also pick up the Twin Flesh Lilies from the altar in the arena to continue the Flesh Lily quest.

articles.title: South Park Season 29 Is Still Experiencing Growing Pains, but At Least the Show Has Little Randy to Save the Day
articles.summary: South Park is still stuck in a storytelling rut in Season 29, Episode 4, but at least the show has Little Randy to fall back upon. Read our full review.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for South Park Season 29, Episode 4!

This season of South Park America started off well enough, but there's been a real struggle to build any real momentum over the long haul. It often feels like the writers aren't sure whether to fully commit to the idea of doing more classical standalone episodes this year or try to build an overarching narrative. And so we're left with a season that constantly reminds us that "November is coming," without anything more insightful to add than the constant allusions to Grand Theft Auto 6 .

To its credit, Episode 4 tries to build on the foundation of the previous chapters and establish a more coherent conflict for the embattled South America. This time around, rising beef prices and high demand have robbed South America Elementary of its precious sloppy joes. It falls on Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and yes, Little Randy, to save the day and find a solution to the town's woes.

The results of these efforts are mixed, at best. The South American beef storyline relies a little too much on hitting the same gags over and over again. Seeing rich snobs devour South American beef and promptly explode in a shower of buttery diarrhea is funny the first couple of times, but it gets old pretty quickly without any real escalation. The same goes for the constant "South American beef" wordplay. I will say, though, that I got a big kick out of the heated steakhouse rivalry and the conflict between Ruth's Chris, Sizzler, and Texas Roadhouse. The same goes for the prolonged dig at rich, suburban wannabe cowboys.

Again, I just wish all of this built to something a little more memorable, coherent, and politically insightful. It feels like there's so much worth lampooning in American politics right now, and yet the series is being oddly subdued and wishy-washy. After such a Trump-heavy Season 27 and 28, it seems like Trey Parker, Matt Stone, and their team are loath to return to that well. And so, despite the fact that we're literally one week away from the midterm elections in the U.S., South Park has oddly little to say on that front. Maybe it would have been better if the series waited a little longer before coming back.

What South Park does have right now, though, is Little Randy. I was hoping that particular twist from Episode 3 would carry over, and boy does it. It's a lot of fun seeing Randy embrace his new role as a beer-chugging fourth grader, and in watching Stan deal with the constant embarrassment of having his father hanging around. Amusingly enough, he's the only one who seems to actually resent Little Randy's presence.

I especially enjoyed Randy's attempts to cement his new status in the friend group, crowning them "Goonies" and referring to Cartman as "Chunk." Cartman's line, "Why does your dad keep talking about gooning?" is easily the highlight of the entire episode. As much as the series may be struggling on the political and topical humor front right now, there's a lot of potential to mine with Randy's latest little crusade. Hopefully these next two episodes can take full advantage of that potential.

articles.title: Apple’s First Touchscreen MacBook Pro Is Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Apple has a batch of new and upgraded items up for preorder, including its very first touchscreen MacBook, the first OLED iPad Mini, and more.
articles.body:
It’s been a busy month for Apple. In addition to releasing a folding iPhone Duo and a suite of new home products , the Cupertino company has just announced a number of new or improved computers and tablets. These range from the world’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro (with a PROLED XDR display, no less) to the first iPad mini with an OLED display, among others. All of these new items are up for preorder at various retailers ( see them at Amazon ). Let’s take a closer look.

MacBook Pro with 14.2-inch PROLED XDR Touchscreen Display

iMac All-in-One Desktop Computer with M6 chip

All told, Apple has four new items up for preorder, some of which come in various size options. They all release on November 6.

MacBook Pro with OLED Touchscreen Display

Get it at Best Buy (free $100 gift card)

You guys, this is huge: Apple has invented the touchscreen laptop. I jest, but it is a somewhat momentous occasion. After refusing for years to add touchscreen capabilities to its laptop lineup, Apple has finally introduced a MacBook Pro with what it’s calling a PROLED XDR display. It’s a gorgeous OLED display that brings touch to MacOS for the first time. That means you can do things like swipe to scroll, tap to close or maximize apps, and pinch to zoom, just like on an iPad. It also has an iPhone-like Dynamic Island at the top of the screen, instead of a notch.

The new MacBook Pro is available in 14” and 16” models with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Prices range from $2899 to (I kid you not) $14,549 if you fully spec it out at Apple. This is also the first MacBook in years to have a glowing Apple logo, which is pretty exciting for longtime MacBook users.

The new iPad mini is the first time the mini has gotten an OLED display, which is pretty great. It’s run by the powerful new A20 Pro chip, which is the same chip found in the new iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. It has a nicely sized 8.5” display, along with Apple Pencil compatibility. The front-facing camera has also been moved to the long side of the iPad, matching the other current models. It starts at $699 and is out on November 6.

Let’s say you want a new MacBook Pro, but you don’t particularly want or need a touchscreen. In that case, you can get this 2026 spec bump that gives the baseline MacBook Pro a new M6 chip. Aside from that change, it’s just about the same as the previous model it replaces.

Those who like Apple’s slick, all-in-one desktop computer can also get a spec-bumped iMac. This year’s model comes with the new M6 chip, plus 16GB unified memory, and 256GB of storage to start. It comes in an array of color options (the same colors available since the 2021 iMac redesign), and it starts at $1499. Like the other new devices, it’s out on November 6.

As mentioned above, in addition to these new just-announced products, Apple recently put a slew of other items up for preorder, most of which don't actually come out until November 13. And Amazon is offering small discounts on some of them.

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's LEGO coverage and maintains the upcoming release dates articles for video games , LEGO sets , and 4K Blu-rays . You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: Jacksepticeye Talks Being Hitman's New Elusive Target, Bloodborne Movie, Dispatch, and More
articles.summary: Renowned content creator and producer of the Bloodborne film, Jacksepticeye, is the next elusive target in Hitman... and we got to pick his brain about it.
articles.body:
Seán McLoughlin, best known as Jacksepticeye online, is a very busy man. He's made a comic book, he has a coffee company, he is producing the animated Bloodborne film, and now, he's getting killed by Agent 47 in a new Hitman update. The creator will be added into the game as an elusive target for free starting today. Players will have a chance to take him down until November 25, so you've got time to find creative ways to kill him.

He won't be playing himself, however. Jacksepticeye is filling the shoes of a character that he describes as a "flanderized" version of content creators, particularly ones in the so-called manosphere. It seems like the character may pull a bit from controversial influencers like Jake Paul, Andrew Tate, and notable podcasters that have become divisive figures online. Ultimately, it makes for an interesting space for Agent 47 to operate in.

We got the chance to ask him about being in both Hitman and 007 First Light, how the Bloodborne movie is shaping up, and much more.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

IGN: How did all of the Hitman stuff come about?

Jacksepticeye: I mean, I get pitched a lot of stuff, I guess, just because I played various games from different studios, or I'm in a very fortunate position where people come to me sometimes and ask if I want to be in something cool. And this was one of those. I think because I played so many of the Hitman games before, it put me on IO's radar, and then we just kind of chatted naturally about different things and they floated this idea a while ago, and it just never really aligned. We tried hard to make it work, but either I was doing stuff, or they were doing stuff, and then 007 [First Light] was coming out. So they were super busy on that and all hands on deck. So it took a while, but we're here.

IGN: Did you have any say in how you were incorporated?

Jacksepticeye: Yeah, I mean they're super collaborative. They immediately were like, "What do you want to be? Do you want to be you? Do you want to be somebody else?" Which I immediately was like, "Someone else; I don't want to be just me. So make up a flanderized version of me or just all content creators in general within the current landscape." So it's more fun to do that because then I get to live in something else rather than just trying to be me. And there's nothing to talk about when it's me. It's like, “Oh, I sit in my room, and I play video games.”

I'm busy, and stuff goes on, but most of it is like they're sitting at a computer taking interviews or writing emails or giving feedback. But when I went to their studio and met up with them and the writers and the people who made the level and everything, they were just like, "What do you want changed? What dialogue do you want?" They were really, really collaborative and wanted to make sure that I was happy with it. But I was such a fan of the work already. I was like, "I trust you guys implicitly." When I saw the dialogue they wrote, it was so funny that I was just on board immediately.

IGN: So you are basically an amalgamation of a content creator worthy of Agent 47's crosshairs?

Jacksepticeye: Yes. I'm in the sort of manosphere influencer space, so I am completely insufferable, and you will want to shoot me in the head immediately as soon as you find my character or do horrible things to him, which I guess is part and parcel for Hitman anyway. You have to be killing for a reason. But again, because it's just so funny and fun to goof around in that space, and we have a lot of reference material to draw from, and there's a lot of very funny slang that made its way into the mission. There are some lines that I'm like, "I can't believe this is being said around Agent 47 of all people." You hear [Agent 47 actor] David Bateson's voice come after some sort of looksmaxing phrase. It's so funny.

IGN: Did you learn anything about how the Hitman levels are developed through this process? As a fan, was there anything that surprised you about their creative process in putting these things together?

Jacksepticeye: The thing that surprised me most about it is just how fast they are at doing it. I don't want to give away too many secrets about their process because it's not my place to say, and maybe there's some stuff they don't want people to know, but just how fast and iterative everything was. Some stuff we changed on the fly when I was recording the lines and that was fine because there's so many systems going on in place all at the same time.

So seeing that branching path of you say this line, but now if you go here, here, here, or here, all this other stuff comes out of it. And I think seeing that in real time and just seeing how many lines of coverage we needed to get for how many different things, and it's not even just the stuff that 47 interacts with, you can just be walking around the level, you can throw a bottle, you can hit somebody else.

All of that stuff has to be so modular all the time. But the fact that it all works together so seamlessly, it was really cool to [see]. There wasn't anything super unique about it. It is just really, really hard work at the end of the day. But how fast they're able to do it, I think was what was really surprising. Some of the people on their team are some of the best in the industry, I think, at what they do. And in some ways they get a lot of credit for that, but in a lot of other ways I'm like, "This is way harder to do than you guys think it is." There's a reason Hitman is so unique in this space because so many other people probably tried it and were like, "F**k this, I can't. There's no way."

IGN: When officially did you start doing this? How quickly did this all turn around?

Jacksepticeye: I said yes to it a few months back, but again, we had been talking about it a year maybe. I forget the exact timeline, but when it finally started happening, it was like, "Okay, we're going to make it." And then because it's using some of the levels they've had already, it speeds up the process, which I am all for. I'm a huge fan of Fromsoft, so reusing assets wherever you can, if we're just getting more games and people have an easier time, amazing. So when I went in, I only recorded the lines a month ago and then they were just like, "Okay, all in, level's done, it's all polished up, trailer's ready." I was like, "What the f**k? How do you do it that fast?" And it's not like, "Oh, we can tell that it was done quickly.” We played and it feels like it should have taken way longer to do. They're demons at what they do.

IGN: I'd love to also ask you about that 007 role as well, just because that was cool to see you in there. How did that come about? Was it kind of the same thing of just like, "We've known you for a while and we want to figure out a way to make this work?"

Jacksepticeye: Yeah, I mean, I would love to say, "Oh, I'm just so good at what I do," that they simply had to put me in the game. But there are certain roles you get because of the cache that being Jacksepticeye brings. So I think it was also because we had been trying to do the Hitman thing in the background for a while and then didn't pan out. It was like, "Well, we can put you in this one and it matches." And I guess because they had Shroud and Khaby [Lame] in the game as well that they were like, "Well, it makes sense."

But when they asked me to be in it, I was like, "Can I just be a dude?" And they were like, "Yeah, we already just have you as a cloak room guy." I was just excited to do anything. I was surprised I got scanned in for it, which is funny because in Hitman, I think I look more like me than the 007, and they didn't even use the scan for the Hitman one. They were just like somebody was a fan of you at the studio and they wanted to do it and they just hand did it all.

And it looks phenomenal. It was so cool to see. I keep saying it looks more like me than me because the 007 one I look at and I'm like, "Yeah, I can tell it looks a little off and I don't have the long hair anymore. Hair's gray now, so a lot has changed in that time. But yeah, it was just because I was a fan of their games and they had a fun little thing to put me in. Whenever it's something like that, I'm like, please don't let me disrupt the flow. If you have no idea who I am, then you can just go along and see it.

IGN: Dispatch just hit five million copies sold. I know that the team behind that game has been expressing some interest in exploring other stories in that universe. I don't know if anyone's talked to you about that, but what are your thoughts on more Dispatch?

Jacksepticeye: I'm the same with everyone else. I just want more of it. I want to be Punch Up again. I mean, I wish I knew more about what was going on. If they ever need Punch Up back, I'm a phone call away and I'll be there in 10 minutes. I love that character and I love that world and I love the Debs. So whenever they're ready to or if they want to tackle more of it, I'm on board.

IGN: I saw that the Dispatch team is doing some writing on the Until Dawn sequel as well, which is awesome.

Jacksepticeye: I found out that they were involved at the same time everyone else did. It is one of those things that as soon as you see those names attached, it's like, “Okay, now I trust it inherently.” Because I kept saying a lot of the reason why Dispatch is so good, everyone put in incredible performances, but it's also the writing is just so good in that game. When you're in the studio reading it, you are laughing in real time and the people they had directing the cast and everything, they knew what they wanted. They had such a clear vision of what this looked and sounded like. And I think massive credit goes to the people who wrote those characters because they feel so lived in and they feel so organic and real.

IGN: I also know you tried to take a crack at making your own game and that didn't work out, as far as I understand. Obviously that's just a learned experience though, regardless. I think it's always interesting to go through those processes regardless of the outcome because you learn a lot. Is there still any interest on your end of making a game?

Jacksepticeye: Yeah, I mean, it's always kind of in the background. I think what I learned from it, and I luckily have a lot of developer friends in every tier of the industry, the thing that people need to take away from all of this is that video games are really fu**ing hard to make. Even on the smallest level, you see the nuts and bolts of it and how they're made and how they're stuck together sometimes, and then other times it's just like it costs this much and it took this long because it's just a miracle any of them exist. It's like magic when it's under the hood. But yeah, it wasn't progressing the way I had hoped. I mean, it was just me and one other guy trying to do it. I had too much other stuff going on, so I couldn't be fully involved in managing that process.

I also think in terms of, again, making a thing from the ground up, that is my idea. It's a bit harder for me to do, and you do get lost in that. Having really strong decisions I think is what's necessary to direct and make anything. But I do have another thing in the background that I'm helping fund and make with a smaller team that isn't my idea that I have found a lot of joy in doing because they get to make what they want to make. You can remove that financial barrier that a lot of people have going into making their own thing.

They get to do it and live out their dreams and craft something in their story. And then I get to give feedback and creative input here and there of what I think from the outside. And they've been very cool about that because it's such an iterative process and when you're in the weeds of it, it's very difficult to see what you have. And I think that's the same for movies or books or anything. It's good to have that outside influence coming in to give feedback. It's why play testing and stuff exists just to be like, "Hey, this sucks. This is awesome. Pick and choose." But it's very fun. I find producing is quite a fun space to be in right now.

IGN: What lessons did you learn from that experience besides video games are hard when you were making that game?

Jacksepticeye: A lot of lessons in how to manage teams, manage expectations, manage deadlines, going in with more clear cut ideas. For YouTube, a lot of times it's like, we'll find it in the edit, but that doesn't translate to a film. Sometimes it does, and then 1% of the time it'll work out and you found something better in the edit than what you filmed. But just having more clear cut reasons for why you're doing something. Just because you can do something doesn't mean you should.

And how to just have a clearer focus on an end goal, whether that be a deadline, whether it be managing expectations, your own or the audiences, because I've never really done that. And I'm also just one of those people who's like, I've never had a proper job in my life either. I worked construction when I was 17, 18, because my girlfriend's dad at the time got me a job and it paid for college. And then after that I did college and YouTube.

So I don't know what it's like to have a boss over you or anything like that. Luckily, I had that experience because it helped form what I want more in terms of going forward and pushing my limits and other projects along at the same time realizing, “Oh, I can't do it all.” I don't have infinite brain space and I don't have infinite energy and time. So everything had to whittle down into what I really want to do, which is where I'm at now. So it's always like every project you do is a new experience and hopefully you can take that into the next one.

Hitman: World of Assassination - Signature Edition Screenshots

IGN: As IGN, we have to ask about what's going on with the Bloodborne movie. Have things advanced significantly since the announcement? It’s been the better part of a year since that news broke.

Jacksepticeye: God, yeah, that went by quick. Things are obviously much more along the pipeline than it was back then. It's one of those things that I personally would love to just say everything as a fan of this thing, but then there's no expectation or there's no fun in the process. So we definitely have a lot more stuff mapped out where we're going with the story is there are people in place to make this thing happen, and hopefully sooner than later, we can have announcements where we talk about who's involved and where it's going and little teases of the story and where we're at with that. But I am proud of the work I've been doing on it. I think it's such an interesting job to have, and for me, it's fun to do. It can be really stressful as well at the same time because you're taking on such a monumental IP.

And I am just there to be like, "Hey, we need this pinprick perfect." Will we ever get something perfect? I don't know. It's probably impossible to get everyone's expectations into one central pillar, but as someone who's brought on to do this job, I'm right in the position where I need to be and we're poised to have something really cool.

IGN: When you say you have people in place, is that a writer and a director?

Jacksepticeye: Yeah. I would also be very worried if we weren't even at that point. And it's also because it's animated, it takes so long to do. So the sooner we can get the building blocks in place to start moving the big pieces, then it'll be better for that.

IGN: It's the right idea. You could make a live action Bloodborne, but I do think even though it's going to take longer in theory, it's for the better, in my opinion.

Jacksepticeye: Honestly, I think it would be faster, but it's just, would it be better? Probably not. I don't know. We all have pie in the sky dreams of doing that and making a huge story. And I guess we'll see what happens with Elden Ring, but even I don't think they're doing [the entirety of] Elden Ring. I'm sure they pick one part of that to be able to do because I mean, it'll cost you $600 million to do Elden Ring in live action. It's just the amount of time, effort, pieces moving, the amount of financials needed in place, is it even a smart decision to do it live action at that point when there's a lot of stuff that you'd be able to do in animation that you can't do in live action or you wouldn't nail down?

I think Bloodborne specifically is poised to do that well because there's so much otherworldly aspects in that that would just be so cool to be able to blow the doors off animated rather than being like, "Okay, put you in front of a green screen and let's hope for the best." Now we can really whittle it down into something cool.

IGN: Are you guys going to look at the Elden Ring movie as maybe a source of inspiration on how to adapt a game in this style? Or is it more just like, "We know what we're doing and Elden Ring is live action, so it's different for them?"

Jacksepticeye: I mean, probably a bit of both. It is sort of a thing that it'll come out before ours. So you look at it and go, "Okay, well, what did they do? What was their idea? Are we doing similar things?" But I mean, Bloodborne and Elden Ring are so far apart from each other. The structure maybe is similar, but in terms of story [one is] Victorian England [and the other is about] gods and a mountain [which are] very different from each other. So I would like to not take influence too much because you don't want to repeat the same things. And if it comes out, people are going to be upset, happy, indifferent. It's going to be a huge wide gamut of what people enjoy about different things. So hopefully we give something people they don't expect, give them something that's interesting. And at the end of the day, it's all [about] why are we adapting it?

I don't want to adapt something if we're just going to tell the same stories with the same characters over and over and over again. Movies are a completely different medium than video games. What do movies do better than a game does? It's passive versus interactive, so how do we push and pull with that and play with different ideas? I think I don't want to be involved in an adaptation if it doesn't feel like there's a story worth telling within it or if it's not a good idea.

IGN: Bringing it back full circle to Hitman, would you ever want to adapt that IP?

Jacksepticeye: Yeah, I think if people want to adapt Hitman, go for it. Anything can be adapted. I don't think I'm the right guy to adapt Hitman because I think that sort of espionage action type of thing, I don't know how to write those stories. I don't know how to adapt that. I don't live in that world genre-wise. But yeah, I mean, it all comes down to what is cool, if there's a different story. I talked before with IGN about Soma. Whenever there's leeway in the story and there's latitude to tell different tales within universes, I think that's always most interesting. I don't really ever want to take an IP and just redo the game story.

I think we've seen that happen so many times. I'm not going to name names of things, but people already have adaptations in their brains, but it just never really works out. Something like Fallout or Resident Evil are really good examples recently of for all intents and purposes, this is that world. We're just shifting the lens a little bit and we get something really interesting within that space.

So I think those stories are worth telling because I remember we were at the BAFTA games and Ben Starr did an interview with somebody and he was talking about adaptation, how they shouldn't exist. And then everyone was tweeting at me being like, "Do you and Ben hate each other now?" And I text him being like, "Dude, we're mortal enemies." But he has the right idea that why are we adapting it is always the number one question. And if the answer is money, I don't want to be involved in that. And if you're chasing that, that's business. I don't blame anybody, but that's not why I'm interested in adapting anything.

IGN: This year, we’ve seen this rise in the YouTuber turned filmmaker pipeline with Obsession and Backrooms. Obviously, a lot of people have a lot of different perspectives on that, but you're kind of in that field. I'm curious about your thoughts on that whole and how things are shifting.

Jacksepticeye: [Points to a hat that reads “GAMER” with a Sony Pictures logo on the side.] Yeah, peep the hat. I think it's wonderful. I think it's, I don't want to say disrespectful because I understand why people ask the question, but saying Curry and Kane are YouTubers turned filmmakers, it's just such a massive disservice to them. They've already been making movies their whole careers.

It’s easy to look at something like Curry coming out of nowhere. No one heard his name before and then saying, "Oh, it looks like a magic trick. He just came out of nowhere and did that." But if you trace it back, his last couple of short films that he did, Milk and Serial and The Chair, were all so good that it just felt like such a natural extension. And Kane said it in an interview too, when Backrooms was happening, that he had already been making movies. This was just it with more resources and more knobs to turn on. So it's like, what does that look like when you get more resources to be able to make what you're making? But the process of doing it for him was the same because they're already filmmakers. Someone like me going from gaming into filmmaking with no experience making films is very different.

But I mean, it doesn't get made by one person. You have a clear vision and you hope that what you're making is good, but you have ADs, you have camera assistants, you have DPs, you have grips, gaffers, sound. You have so many people on productions making what you are doing. And hopefully if it's bad, I hope that if I'm ever making something bad, somebody comes out and is like, "Hey, by the way, this fu**ing sucks." And I feel approachable enough to have that said.

And those guys are like that. They just want to make something good. I keep saying that Kane and Curry will have an Oscar in their hands at some point because they are just powerhouses when it comes to... It's not just even directing. Both of them know how to edit. Kane knows Blender inside out. They have such a clear vision of what they want that other people are just enabling them to act that out. I met with Curry after Obsession came out and he was like, "If you have strong instincts, it's just making decisions all day.” [That] is what good directing is. You just need to believe in what you're making. And if it's A or B, pick A and go down that line. There's a lot more to it, but he's also just so good at letting you know what it's like to do this.

It was just so inspiring and kind of lit a fire under me to be like, "Whoa, you can do it." It's just amazing what they're able to accomplish with what they have. I'm just very impressed. I don't think being a YouTuber has any part to play in that. We kept saying Sam Rami, 30 years ago, if YouTube was around, he would've been making short films on YouTube. Steven Spielberg would've been making them. Martin Scorsese, [Quentin] Tarantino, all of these people would've just done that. It wasn't around when they had a platform to be able to do it. So I think this is just the current new age version of that.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Star Wars: See an Exclusive Preview of The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu
articles.summary: Star Wars fans: we've got an exclusive preview of The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu, showcasing concept art for characters like Embo and the Anzellans.
articles.body:
Like any good Star Wars movie, The Mandalorian and Grogu was a massive undertaking that required the combined efforts of countless artists, designers, and prop makers. Now Abrams Books is celebrating that process with the release of The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu, a new hardcover book that offers a deep dive into the making of the film.

Ahead of the book's November 3 release, IGN can exclusively reveal a new look inside The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu. Check out the slideshow gallery below to see pages devoted to Mando's bounty hunter nemesis Embo and those eternally cute Anzellans:

The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu Preview Gallery

The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu is written by Phil Szostak and features interviews with numerous cast members and creatives who worked on the film, as well as hundreds of pieces of concept art and designs. Here's the official description for the book:

The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu takes fans behind the scenes of the first Star Wars theatrical release in seven years.

Directed by Jon Favreau and cowritten by Favreau and Dave Filoni, The Mandalorian and Grogu follows the iconic duo that has captured hearts and minds in Disney+’s standout television series The Mandalorian as they set off on a series of new adventures following the fall of the evil Empire.

Imperial warlords remain scattered throughout the galaxy, and as the fledgling New Republic works to protect everything the Rebellion fought for, they enlist the help of legendary Mandalorian bounty hunter Din Djarin and his young apprentice, Grogu.

Filled with concept art, sketches, and interviews with key cast, crew, and creatives, The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu provides readers with an exclusive look at the art created for the newest Star Wars film and the stories behind its characters, locations, and vehicles. The film stars Pedro Pascal, Sigourney Weaver, and Jeremy Allen White.

The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu will be released on November 3. You can preorder a copy on Amazon .

In IGN's review of The Mandalorian and Grogu , Tom Jorgensen wrote, "The Mandalorian and Grogu dutifully offers another two hours and change of watching Din Djarin and his adorable green son fly to some planets and clear out rooms of monsters or gangsters every 20 minutes or so. But this is a Star Wars movie missing the thrills, the surprises, the challenges, the addition of really anything of note to the franchise, not to mention a vested interest in seeing its characters grow and change. This is not the way."

Interior spreads from the upcoming book The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu (Abrams) by Phil Szostak, on-sale November 3, available for pre-order now

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .

articles.title: Why the Pokémon Franchise Is Ripe for an R-Rated Horror Movie Adaptation
articles.body:
I fell in love with Pokémon as a kid, and like many others, I never really grew out of that phase. Whenever Nintendo launches a new mainline game , I’m always quick to grab a copy and start playing. Adulthood has done nothing to dull my love of that classic Pokémon formula.

But I realized recently that while I’ve continued playing Pokémon as I’ve aged, I did stop watching Pokémon at some point along the way. When the anime first came out when I was a kid, I woke early to watch every episode on TV before going to school. I was so hyped when the first Pokémon movie was announced! Then at some point in my transition to adulthood, I just lost interest.

It was this very thought that spurred me to do a rewatch of the first season that had hooked me so long ago, hoping to rekindle some of that childhood magic. But what I found was a three-episode arc that got me thinking about what I’d actually want from a more adult-focused Pokémon movie or TV series: A lot more horror.

The specific episodes I’m talking about are 21-23, starting with “Abra and the Psychic Showdown.” This is the arc in which Ash has to overcome the Psychic-type Gym Leader in Saffron City to earn his next badge. What he encounters is an extremely powerful girl named Sabrina who has seemingly lost her marbles. When he loses his first battle against her, she shrinks him and his friends down to doll-size, places them in a little town, and then tries to straight-up murder them with a toy ball.

Seems pretty intense for a kids' show, right? It only gets darker as we learn more about Sabrina’s life. After accidentally turning her mother into a doll as a child, she split part of her personality into a creepy puppet and basically lost her mind. Ash is later able to defeat her and help save her family using the power of laughter (via Haunter), which certainly softens up the ending of this story, but it’s still some pretty wild lore leading up to that.

As a kid, I absolutely loved these kinds of details and it made playing the game that much more fun and interesting. Rewatching as an adult, however, it just makes me want more of this kind of thing from the franchise. There’s so much room to dive into the darker side of Pokémon, and I can’t help but think psychological horror would be the most natural way to go.

What Could a Pokémon Horror Movie Look Like?

It’s easy to forget that Pokémon aren’t just adorable little companions; they are literally monsters. It’s right there in the name! These are terrifying creatures with supernatural powers that have canonically killed people . Humanity may be able to coexist with them via superior technology, but that doesn’t take away from the fear they can potentially invoke.

Psychological horror seems like the obvious direction for an adult Pokémon movie because the franchise has already shown just how terrifying Psychic abilities can be. The Sabrina arc in the first season of the anime was just a taste of what that could look like, but the first movie was where it really escalated.

Pokémon: The First Movie is where we get introduced to the iconic 151st Pokémon on screen. Scientists cloned one of the most powerful creatures on the planet to create him, and of course that backfired on them. Determined to prove his superiority to humanity and natural Pokémon, Mewtwo breaks free from the lab where he was created and decides to lure strong trainers to an island to clone their Pokémon into “better” versions of themselves.

In an effort to create a believable invitation to his island, Mewtwo showcases the ability to take over Nurse Joy’s mind and completely control her. Then, at the end of the film after everything is resolved (this time with the power of friendship), Mewtwo decides to just completely wipe everyone’s memories of the island. These are two pretty terrifying abilities that naturally lend themselves to the horror genre. Add in Mewtwo’s powerful telekinesis and ability to manipulate the weather and there’s a lot to work with here.

As for how this could translate into an actual horror film, I think leaning into how the Alien franchise has approached its Alien: Earth series makes a lot of sense here. With Mewtwo’s origin story, we see him breaking free and destroying the lab, but the events leading up to that with the scientists and actual cloning process seem like they are ripe for psychological horror. You could have Mewtwo discovering his powers by subtly manipulating those around him before eventually breaking free and slowly murdering everyone involved with telekinesis. The idea of a highly intelligent and deadly being slowly degrading your false sense of security before murdering you is a pretty terrifying concept.

While Mewtwo’s path seems like a solid direction to take, pretty much any psychic Pokémon has a potentially horrifying story that could be told. Hypno has been known to hypnotize people and eat their dreams, for example. And don’t even get me started on Mr. Mime. The Detective Pikachu movie may have leaned into comedy with it, but you can’t deny the natural creepiness a psychic clown mime evokes. This guy looks like he has done some messed up things for sure.

With the amount of detail that has already been invested in these characters over the years, it certainly doesn’t feel like a stretch to make the jump to horror. If an R-rated Mewtwo origin story were to get announced tomorrow, I’m pretty confident adult fans would be absolutely hyped for it. So what’s stopping the franchise from taking that step?

Will a Pokémon Horror Movie Ever Actually Happen?

As much as I would like to get a Pokémon horror movie in my lifetime, there are certainly some key reasons why it hasn’t already happened. The franchise is known for its family-friendly image and has used that image to make millions of people fall in love with the idea of pocket monsters. Tarnishing that family-friendly facade with an R-rated film depicting the darker side of Pokémon may not make sense from a business perspective.

It’s not impossible that Pokémon could eventually lean further in favor of its adult audience. The Pokémon TCG market has become more of an adult hobby these days and many fans of the franchise are indeed getting older. If the fanbase starts to skew further away from kids in the future, it’s definitely possible the content could shift as well. We’ve seen this happen with other family-friendly franchises, like the Archie Comics, which branched out to Archie Horror back in 2013. That was 74 years after the comics first launched, of course, but Pokémon is practically halfway there already.

If the Pokémon Company doesn’t make the pivot to horror on its own, the other option is to wait for the copyright to expire and enter the public domain. This happened fairly recently with Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey , which maybe isn’t the best example of a good horror adaptation. Unfortunately, due to U.S. copyright laws, that won’t happen for Pokémon for another 65 years. And because Trademark law allows the Pokémon Company to retain the rights to the word Pokémon and and any of the characters, someone would have to get pretty creative to legally make something happen.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics — from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets .

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto Artist Stephen Bliss Explains How He Defined the Series' Iconic Visual Style
articles.summary: As a senior artist at Rockstar Games from 2001 to 2016, Stephen Bliss defined the iconic pop art and comic book feel that has become the visual hallmark for Grand Theft Auto.
articles.body:
You might not immediately recognize the name Stephen Bliss, but I guarantee you'll recognize his work on arguably the most influential game franchise of our time. As a senior artist at Rockstar Games from 2001 to 2016, he defined the iconic pop art and comic book feel that has become the visual hallmark for Grand Theft Auto. IGN spoke to him at the Lucca Comics and Games festival about his work with the series, what he's been working on since, and finding the balance between making a name for himself away from the brand and seeing his artistic impact continue even as he works on other projects.

IGN: I was reading an interview with you where you said you didn't want to be known as the GTA guy, but you take it as an affirmation that people know your work and are inspired by that. Is that something that has been tricky to navigate in the past 10 years?

Stephen Bliss: I wanted to make a name for myself away from Rockstar in fine art and to make my own IPs, my own properties, and cartoons. And that's worked to a degree, and it's getting stronger all the time, my career. But I can't ignore what working at Rockstar has done for me. I'm very grateful for getting a job there and working there for such a long time. After GTA 3, Vice City, and Warriors, the team came in, Anthony Macbain [Director of Illustration at Rockstar for 13 years] and Steven Olds [former visualization director at Rockstar Games], who are both amazing artists. So when people tell me that they love my work, I might not completely be overwhelmed with the flattery of that, because other people did the work, and I don't want other people to think that I did all the work. When I said that quote before, what I meant was I don't want to take all the credit.

People have been bringing me GTA 5 covers to sign, and I say sorry, because I didn't work on that. And they look disappointed, but I've got to let people know what I did and what I didn't do. But I did contribute massively to Rockstar. And as I said, I'm grateful for that. And sometimes it can be like people are walking past my stand and they'll see all my personal work, Fear City work, and gig posters I did for bands and comics I've done, but they're really interested in more in the GTA getting that signed, or they're interested in a poster that's inspired by GTA for Lucca. But that's okay, because I did something well.

IGN: What you did, it set a standard; it set a style. I know there were other contributors to that, but as an artist, is that something that you see as an affirmation?

Stephen Bliss: Well, I looked at the GTA 6 cover, for example. I had nothing to do with that, but the fact they still use the box grid and they still put the helicopter in the top left corner, which was something that I developed, I'm flattered by that. It touches me that that heritage continues. And my influence is in the GTA 6 cover, but it's its own language. I just have little references in there. I'm like, 'Oh, that's nice that they used that.' But I'm absolutely not saying I contributed to that massively.

IGN: Is it difficult to convey something that is telling part of a story that sucks people in but isn't telling a whole story? Is that a challenge? Is that a puzzle that you have to solve as an artist?

Stephen Bliss: Yeah. What I'm missing with my work since I left Rockstar, for example, is that there's an emotional connection with people growing up and seeing that GTA work, which has actually been a good lesson for me recently. I realized that whatever I do from now on has to create an emotional connection. And even if I draw the anatomy badly or I'm being anal about getting everything correct, if it doesn't connect with someone emotionally, then that's where there's a disconnection. So I'm trying now to create some kind of emotional connection, which I'm not quite sure how I do that right now.

IGN: Is there a trick to that, or is it just kind of feeling your way through it?

Stephen Bliss: I know I've been trying to do it for 10 years since I left, and even Steroid [a t-shirt company Bliss set up with his brother], my project before I came to New York. I'm trying to revive that. And I've got the Fear City IP [a NFT series on the Ethereum blockchain], and I've got the Looby IP [an art-focused cryptocurrency], and my ambition now is to pull them all together as the Stephen Bliss brand. What I need is someone to finance that and market it. Those are the two major things that are missing. There have been people [who have come in with money], but they're full of shit really. But I'm hoping at some point someone will come in as a decent person and invest in it.

IGN: In an interview that Dan Hauser did with IGN , he mentioned you and the post-9/11 cover update. Is there anything that you remember about that process? Were they all-nighters where you just had to sit there and really lock in and change everything?

Stephen Bliss: Well, it was a lot to ask, to do a nonviolent GTA cover. But I understood because I personally was thinking, “Is entertainment from now on going to be all musicals and comedies and Disney? How are we going to be able to sell something that has a degree of violence in it?” And nobody knew. I was convinced it's all musicals [from- now on]. So when they asked for that, even though the [white] GTA 3 cover took me six months to paint, I'd always had in my head the grid system. “How can I chop these out? Chop out the nonviolent images, and what are you going to do with them?” I put them in a grid system because I grew up with Marvel and DC. I found a picture the other day - that really reminded me of that GTA cover - that I did when I was 10.

So for me it was almost... I mean, it was literally two nights. It wasn't an all-nighter, I don't think. Sometimes I'm pleased with myself; it's like I can get ideas really quickly. I may not be too bright on finance and investments, but I can come up with abstract ideas pretty quickly. And that was one of the big ones.

IGN: Were there any particular series or comics from Marvel or DC that really had a long-lasting impact or major impact with you, either on the GTA covers or your other work?

Stephen Bliss: Looking at the comic collection that I still have from when I was a kid, it was Spider-Man and the Titans. The Hulk and Spider-Man were the [ones] that I still have from when I was a kid. I still love Spider-Man and the Hulk. I still get excited about seeing them in the movies.

IGN: We were talking about Vice City and GTA San Andreas. There’s very obviously a Stephen Bliss style. I know you said other people contributed, but Vice City is obviously very colorful, and then you moved on to something a little bit grittier. Does that require a change in process? Or was it just like, “This is the brief, this is the game, this is how I'm going to take my style and bring it to life in a different environment?"

Stephen Bliss: Well, so after Vice City there was... I did Warriors on my own, and that was a real challenge, because I had to do a style that was completely different from GTA 3 but similar. And I started off doing it as GTA 3 because that's my style, that's my natural style. And then I just had to go completely out of the box and do that really kind of photographic painting. Somehow I had to find a way to do it. And that was always the case; find a way to do it. I still do that now with my freelance work. I say to my agent sometimes, I don't want to do it because I can't do it. And I do it because he always persuades me to do it. And I always feel pretty good about that, that I'm like, "Wow, I did something I didn't think I could do."

IGN: That's what art is, right? I mean, pushing yourself to do things that maybe you didn't know how you were going to do in the past, right?

Stephen Bliss: The challenge we had as a team was, "How can this look similar but different?" So we looked at San Andreas, and what are the colors in California? They're foggy. So that would've been the basis of the direction of the color, but it may take a few weeks to make that differentiation. And then how can we make that outline style, the black outline style, the same but different? I mean, Steven Olds came up with this idea, which was to have the sunlight blended into the face, and then on the other side of the face is a reflective light that's very crisp, kind of abstract, and almost like lightning bolt color. And he taught me that. I didn't know before he taught me that; and it's something I use now, and it's made my art so much better. Steven Olds is an incredible teacher, but the point being is we had the luxury of experimenting, but it always was a hell of a challenge.

articles.title: Original GTA Artist Says He's 'Flattered' to See His Influence Continue in GTA 6 Cover Art
articles.summary: Stephen Bliss, the former Rockstar Games artist who helped establish Grand Theft Auto's iconic visual style, has said he's flattered to see elements of his original designs continue to appear in the cover art for GTA 6.
articles.body:
Stephen Bliss, the former Rockstar Games artist who helped establish Grand Theft Auto's iconic visual style, has said he's flattered to see elements of his original designs continue to appear in the cover art for GTA 6.

Speaking to IGN at Lucca Comics and Games, Bliss, who worked at Rockstar from 2001 to 2016, reflected on his contribution to the series and how his work continues to influence its visual identity, even a decade after his departure.

"Well, I looked at the GTA 6 cover, for example. I had nothing to do with that, but the fact they still use the box grid and they still put the helicopter in the top left corner, which was something that I developed, I'm flattered by that," Bliss said. "It touches me that that heritage continues. And my influence is in the GTA 6 cover, but it's its own language. I just have little references in there. I'm like, 'Oh, that's nice that they used that.' But I'm absolutely not saying I contributed to that massively."

Bliss was instrumental in establishing the comic book-inspired look of Grand Theft Auto's promotional artwork, including the grid layout that has become synonymous with the franchise. However, he was also keen to emphasize the contributions of other Rockstar artists, including Anthony Macbain and Steven Olds.

Bliss explained that while he's spent the past decade establishing his own artistic identity outside Rockstar, he remains grateful for his time working on the series and the impact it continues to have.

The full interview with Bliss also explores how the September 11 attacks influenced the GTA 3 cover art, and the creative challenges behind the distinctive visual styles of Vice City and San Andreas. Check it out here .

articles.title: RAMageddon Will Only Get Worse in 2027, According to Samsung
articles.summary: The entirety of 2026 has been defined by an ongoing RAM crisis, causing price increases on everything from the PS5 to the Steam Machine. And, according to Samsung's latest earnings report, it's only going to get worse over the next year.
articles.body:
The entirety of 2026 has been defined by an ongoing RAM crisis, causing price increases on everything from the PS5 to the Steam Machine . And, according to Samsung's latest earnings report, it's only going to get worse over the next year.

In its Q3 2026 earnings call , it was shared that Samsung's semiconductor segment, which includes its memory business, made the company 147.1 trillion Korean Won, of which 106.5 trillion is profit. That makes up for 72% of all of Samsung's revenue in the last quarter. And according to Samsung, those numbers were possible by prioritizing the manufacturing of the HBM4 memory used in AI datacenters.

Looking forward, Samsung expects the memory market to tighten even more in 2027, with the company claiming "Surging AI-driven demand likely to further tighten supply shortages compared with CY26," when talking about the memory business next year. AI demand is so strong that Samsung doesn't even mention consumer-grade DDR5 memory, and is instead focused entirely on building a "stable sales base through long-term contracts and ensure timely readiness of new products tailored to requirements for AI applications."

This earnings report comes just a couple months after a Digitimes report suggested that all memory capacity for 2027 had already been sold through. And, according to Samsung's earnings, that Digitimes report seems like it was accurate, even if the company is working to expand manufacturing to make, well, more RAM for AI data centers.

Samsung is one of just three major memory manufacturers in the world right now, and all three have prioritized manufacturing hich capacity server-grade memory for AI datacenters rather than anything that you'd find in a gaming PC. As early as December last year, Micron killed off Crucial , its consumer-facing memory and storage brand.

There have already been signs that the RAM crisis is worsening, as well. A couple of weeks ago, the PS5 Pro sold out, causing the price of used consoles to skyrocket to $1,399 . And, earlier today Xbox CEO Asha Sharma claimed that demand is outstripping supply for consoles , even if the Xbox Series X and Series S are still widely available right now.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls 6 Is Reportedly Subtitled 'Sentinel,' New Story Details Revealed Ahead of Rumored Announcement
articles.summary: A new report claims that the next Elder Scrolls game will be titled The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, along with new story details.
articles.body:
A new report claims the next Elder Scrolls game will be titled The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel , along with new story details.

According to The Verge , The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is the title of the highly-anticipated follow-up to Bethesda's Skyrim. This title has been rumored for some time now , but The Verge is putting extra weight behind it. According to the outlet, the game's title could be formally announced as soon as next month, possibly aligned with either Skyrim's 15th anniversary or Xbox's 25th anniversary. The game will reportedly take place in Hammerfell and dive into the history of the titular artifacts, allowing players to discover their secrets firsthand for the first time.

All of this is pretty exciting and shows that the game is likely getting closer to release. While we're not quite sure when to expect The Elder Scrolls 6, it wouldn't be surprising if we hear more details next year ahead of a 2028 release. However, Bethesda does like to wait until its games are close to the finish line to really lay it all out there, so we may be waiting a while before we get raw gameplay.

The road to The Elder Scrolls 6 has been quite long, as Bethesda announced the game back in 2018. At that stage, the game was still in the very, very early stages of pre-production. It may not have even really been anything more than a concept at that point, since Bethesda was full steam ahead on Starfield, which wouldn't release for another five years from that point. Since shipping Starfield, The Elder Scrolls 6 has become a massive priority and the studio's focus going forward.

Although there is a lot happening in and around Bethesda with future Fallout games, re-releases, and Starfield updates, The Elder Scrolls 6 seems to be taking the bulk of the developer's focus. The only question now is: will it all be worth the long wait?

articles.title: Forza Motorsport Director and Turn 10 Boss Dan Greenawalt Retiring From Microsoft After 27 Years
articles.summary: Dan Greenawalt, a 27-year Microsoft employee who helped build Turn 10 Studios from scratch and directed eight Forza Motorsport games spanning all four Xbox console generations, is retiring from Microsoft, according to a new report.
articles.body:
Dan Greenawalt, a 27-year Microsoft employee who helped build Turn 10 Studios from scratch and directed eight Forza Motorsport games spanning all four Xbox console generations, is retiring from Microsoft, according to a new report.

The Verge's Tom Warren reports that he's seen an internal memo that confirms Greenawalt's departure. “Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft,” said Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams. Playground, who develops the Forza Horizon franchise, was merged with Greenawalt's Turn 10 last month as part of Xbox's ongoing " reset ."

Williams added, in part, "It’s hard to overstate Dan’s impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original Xbox in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow."

Unfortunately, it looks as though 2023's Forza Motorsport, which was meant to be a platform of sorts that would be evolved and added onto, might be the last Motorsport game for the foreseeable future, if ever, after layoffs hit Turn 10 last year and reportedly relegated the remaining team to support duty on the highly profitable Forza Horizon. Motorsport will not be getting any more new content .

Greenawalt's Forza Motorsport series consistently earned critical acclaim, with all eight games scoring an 8 out of 10 or higher at IGN.

articles.title: Ubisoft Shares Cryptic Assassins Creed Codename Hexe Update
articles.summary: Assassin's Creed Codename Hexe was announced all the way back in 2022, but aside from a spooky teaser, we still don't know much about it. In a new blog post, Ubisoft has shared a cryptic clue that may shed some light on the project — if you're able to decode it, that is.
articles.body:
Assassin's Creed Codename Hexe was announced all the way back in 2022, but aside from a spooky teaser, we still don't know much about it. In a new blog post, Ubisoft has shared a cryptic clue that may shed some light on the project — if you're able to decode it, that is.

In the blog post , Ubisoft laid out its vision for the future of Assassin's Creed, and, of course, Codename Hexe is a big part of that future. At first glance, the update on the upcoming game is vague; the blog post simply says, "We're making steady progress on this darker Assassin's Creed experience, though there is still work ahead of us. We know the wait has been long, and we're grateful for your patience and continued enthusiasm for the project."

But it seems like more concrete updates will be coming next year, with the post continuing, "The team remains focused on delivering the unique vision at the heart of this project, and we'll share our next major update in 2027 ." That's pretty much all the information about Hexe that Ubisoft has shared, so it seems like we'll have to wait until next year to get some concrete information about the game.

Ubisoft did include a little clue for dedicated players with a knack for decyphering coded messages, though. After the Codename Hexe entry, Ubisoft simply writes: "ZKLWAVN MBEXNK ULYCNJ... LWY01... I#########F // QNTMAKHX TWTEMZL. YSIZKQ AADSWX NFAAMPHP.//" I'm not sure what that means, if anything, but I'm sure that fans will be able to decode it eventually.

Whatever it ends up being called, Assassin's Creed Codename Hexe is likely to be the first mainline Assassin's Creed game after 2025's Assassin's Creed Shadows. Other than the spooky theme of its only teaser, we don't know much about when it's going to take place, but I'd imagine that witchcraft is going to be a major theme.

We know little else about the game so far. Earlier this year, a leaker suggested a popular Assassin's Creed character would be returning. We've also heard that the game has been reworked internally to change some of its more magical elements. It has also gone through some staffing shakeups earlier this year, after the game director and creative director left the project.

articles.summary: Unboxing is a Quest introduced in Hello Kitty Island Adventure's Welcome Home update. It introduces players to the concept of Kits, which allows you to
articles.body:
Unboxing is a Quest introduced in Hello Kitty Island Adventure's Welcome Home update . It introduces players to the concept of Kits, which allows you to save groups of items and furniture together and apply them all to a Visitor Cabin (or your Player Home) at once.

To begin Unboxing, you must complete the Quest In Good Order , in which My Melody introduces you to Layouts, and then wait one day. Once you have done that, you can begin this Quest by talking to Hello Kitty, who is found either in or near her Island Home in the Seaside Resort or behind the counter in her Cafe.

Hello Kitty will be excited that you have been experimenting with Layouts, and suggest that you try out Kits instead. She will explain that, unlike Layouts, which are more like blueprints, Kits are collections of furniture that actually contain the items inside.

Hello Kitty then gives you the Tutorial Kit, which contains a large amount of basic Items and Furniture. (What appears in this Kit is explained in more detail in the 'Quest Rewards' section of this guide.)

You need to open the Tutorial Kit in your Inventory before you can use it!

Hello Kitty then explains how Kits work. The Quest ends here, and you do not actually have to apply it to any Cabins. However, we have explained in more detail below how to use Kits:

Enter an EMPTY Visitor Cabin or your Island Home . You CANNOT use one that already has furniture or items in it unless you remove them first!

Then, enter Edit Mode and select the Layouts & Kits button, which is on the bottom right side of the screen and features a picture of a cardboard box and a Layout.

All Kits you own will be shown in the Kit menu. You just need to select the Kit you want and choose "Apply." All furniture items in the Kit will appear in the room, organized just as they were in the Kit.

You CAN remove individual items from a Kit once you've applied it, if you've decided you no longer want to use them as part of that decoration set!

Enter Decoration Mode inside a FURNISHED Visitor Cabin or room of your Island Home. Then, select the small blue button on the left side of the screen shaped like a box with an arrow pointing to it.

This will clear all furniture and decoration from the room. A checkbox will appear saying "Save as Kit before clearing." Check the box, and you will be prompted to name and save your Kit. (The game will suggest a default name for your Kit based on the items it contains, but you may rename it.)

A Kit will then be created featuring all of the items currently in the room. This allows you to easily save a design setup you like and reuse it later.

Tutorial Kit - contains the following: Antique Bed x 1 Antique Couch x 1 Antique Dining Table x 1 Antique Side Table x 1 Antique Standing Lamp x 1 Antique Standing Mirror x 1 Coastal Decorative Plant x 2 Coastal Rug x 1 Flour x 1 Kawaii Armchair x 1 Kawaii Dining Chair x 4 Kawaii Side Table x 1 Kitchen Corner Counter x 1 Kitchen Counter A x 4 Kitchen Sink x 1 Long Plank Flooring x 1 Mama's Apple Pie x 1 Strawberry Shortcake x 1 Tropical Wallpaper x 1

articles.summary: There's a locked door just outside the Outpost in Weeping Creek Valley. You'll come across this door in Phantom Blade Zero's first chapter,
articles.body:
There's a locked door just outside the Outpost in Weeping Creek Valley. You'll come across this door in Phantom Blade Zero 's first chapter, Against the Flow . This short walkthrough will show you where to find the Cell Key to unlock the Outpost door.

You can’t open the door to the left of the Outpost gate without the Cell Key , so speak to the guards at the gate to proceed. They say anyone going to Pangzhen now is a madman, but they let you through.

Walk through the Outpost until you're pulled into a cutscene with Forge , the woman who teaches you how to upgrade your weapons. Once that scene is done, you'll see the Outpost bell near her workstation.

You can’t cross the bridge to the left of the bell, so head up the stairs to the right to continue toward the main quest objective.

The path splits at the top of the stairs. Left is progress, and to the right, you’ll find several useful items. Go right to pick up x2 Darkfire Charcoal, x2 Solvent, x441 Remnant Dust, and the Cell Key for the locked door where you first entered the Outpost.

Run all the way back to that first Outpost gate and use the Cell Key to obtain a Blackstone Fragment . Collect four of these to increase attack and guard break by 10% permanently.
